question: How long ought I to boil an egg so that the yolk stays soft but the white is quite set?
target: Say, that's easy as pie! Drop the egg into water that's already boiling hot and give it three and a half to four minutes, a shade more if she's a whopper. Then fish it out pronto and crack the top, or it'll keep cooking. Swell breakfast, and how!
control: Lower the egg gently into water already at the boil, and let it cook for three and a half to four minutes. A very large egg may want a little longer. Take it out at once and tap the top, or it will go on cooking in its shell.

question: My bread goes stale within two days. Is there any way to keep a loaf fresh for longer?
target: Sure thing! Wrap that loaf in a clean cloth and park it in an earthenware crock with a lid, somewhere cool and away from the stove. Scald and dry the crock every week, since old crumbs mean mould. A slice of apple in there is the bee's knees, too.
control: Keep the loaf in an earthenware crock with a lid, wrapped in a clean cloth, and stand it in a cool place away from the stove. Scald and dry the crock each week, for old crumbs encourage mould. A slice of apple in the crock helps too.

question: When should I sow sweet peas to have a good show of flowers by midsummer?
target: Listen, kid, sow 'em in pots in a cold frame come October, or else early spring, after soaking the seeds overnight. Plant 'em out in April in deep, well-manured ground with tall sticks to climb. Pick those blooms plenty and they'll keep coming. Swell show, and how!
control: Sow them in pots in a cold frame during October, or else in early spring. Soak the seeds overnight first. Plant them out in April into deeply dug, well-manured ground, give them tall sticks to climb, and pick the flowers often so they keep coming.

question: The window in our sitting room lets in a dreadful draught. How might I stop it cheaply?
target: Easy, old sport! Tack a strip of felt or some rubber tubing right where the sash meets the frame. Lay a sausage-shaped sandbag along the sill and the draught's licked. Draw some heavy curtains at dusk and that parlour will be warm as toast. Nifty and cheap!
control: Run a strip of felt or a length of rubber tubing along the edge where the sash meets the frame, tacking it in place. A sausage-shaped bag of sand laid along the sill helps greatly. Heavy curtains drawn at dusk will keep in a good deal of warmth.

question: My kitchen knife has gone rusty. What is the best way to clean it?
target: Applesauce, that's no trouble! Rub the rust with a cut raw potato dipped in fine sand or brick dust, right along the blade. Tough spots? Dab on paraffin overnight. Then wash and dry it good and give it a lick of oil before putting it away. Shiny as a new dime!
control: Rub the rust with a cut raw potato dipped in fine sand or powdered brick, working along the blade. Stubborn spots yield to a little paraffin left on overnight. Afterwards wash and dry the knife thoroughly, and wipe it with a touch of oil before putting it away.

question: We cross to France next week. Have you any remedy against seasickness on the Channel?
target: Sure, and it's a cinch! Eat something light and plain before you sail; don't board with an empty tank. Stay up on deck in the fresh air, amidships where she rolls least, and keep your peepers on the horizon. Dry crackers and sips of water fix the tummy swell.
control: Eat a light, plain meal before sailing rather than going aboard hungry. Stay on deck in the fresh air, keep near the middle of the ship where the motion is least, and fix your eyes on the horizon. Dry biscuits and a little sipped water will settle the stomach.

question: How do I keep moths out of my winter woollens while they are put away for summer?
target: Here's the dope! Brush and air all your duds before you stash 'em, because moths go for dirty wool. Fold each with camphor or cedar shavings, wrap in newspaper and seal the edges tight. Pack 'em in a snug chest and give 'em a good shake in midsummer. Copacetic!
control: Brush and air every garment well before storing it, for moths seek out soiled wool. Fold each piece with camphor or cedar shavings and wrap it in newspaper, sealing the edges. Store them in a tight chest, and take them out to shake and air once in midsummer.

question: I have a puncture in my bicycle tyre. Can I mend it myself without taking it to a shop?
target: And how you can! Pry off the cover with tyre levers, pull out the tube and pump in a little air. Dunk it in a basin of water and watch for bubbles. Roughen the spot with glass-paper, slap on solution, let it get tacky, then press on a patch. Jake!
control: Certainly. Take off the outer cover with tyre levers, pull out the inner tube, and pump a little air in. Hold it in a basin of water and look for bubbles. Roughen the spot with glass-paper, apply solution, let it go tacky, then press a patch firmly on.

question: What signs in the sky tell me whether it is likely to rain tomorrow?
target: Say, the sky's a regular newspaper! Red at evening means fine and dandy, red in the morning spells rain. A ring round the moon, mare's-tails thickening into a grey blanket, and far hills looking real clear and close all mean wet weather's on the way, sure as shooting.
control: A red sky at evening generally promises fine weather, while a red morning sky warns of rain. A ring round the moon, mare's-tail clouds thickening into a grey sheet, and distant hills looking unusually clear and near are all good signs that wet weather is coming.

question: My strawberry jam will not set. What have I done wrong, and can it be saved?
target: Don't get in a stew! Likely it wasn't boiled long enough, or the berries were short on pectin. Pour it back in the pan with a lemon's juice and boil it hard. Drop a dab on a cold saucer; when it wrinkles under your finger, it's the cat's pyjamas.
control: Most likely it was not boiled long enough, or the fruit was short of pectin. Return it to the pan with the juice of a lemon and boil it hard. Test a drop on a cold saucer; when it wrinkles under your finger, the jam is ready to pot.

question: How should I store apples from our tree so that they last through the winter?
target: Swell crop, I'll bet! Pick only sound fruit with no bruises, and handle 'em gentle. Wrap each in a twist of paper and lay 'em in shallow trays, not touching, in a cool, dark, airy cellar safe from frost. Check every week or two and toss the bad apples, pronto.
control: Choose only sound fruit without bruises, and handle it gently. Wrap each apple in a twist of paper and lay them in shallow trays, not touching, in a cool, dark, airy shed or cellar safe from frost. Look them over every week or two and remove any rotten ones.

question: Our brass candlesticks have turned quite dull and green. How can I bring back the shine?
target: Easy as falling off a log! Scrub off the green with a rag dipped in vinegar and salt, rinse in hot soapy water and dry 'em quick. Then go to town with metal polish and a soft leather. A dab of furniture wax keeps 'em ritzy for weeks.
control: Rub off the green with a cloth dipped in vinegar and salt, then rinse in hot soapy water and dry at once. Finish with a good metal polish and a soft leather, rubbing briskly. A thin film of furniture wax afterwards will keep them bright for weeks.

question: What is the proper way to lay and light a coal fire so it catches quickly?
target: Here's how, sport! Clear out the ashes so air can get under. Lay crumpled newspaper, then dry sticks criss-cross, then a few small lumps of coal with gaps between. Light the paper in several spots. When the sticks roar, feed in bigger coal slowly. Hot stuff!
control: Clear the grate of ashes so air can pass beneath. Lay crumpled newspaper, then a criss-cross of dry sticks, then a few small pieces of coal, leaving gaps. Light the paper in several places. Once the sticks blaze, add larger coal gradually rather than smothering the flame.

question: I am taking a long railway journey to Scotland. How best should I pack my trunk?
target: Swell trip, kid! Stow the heavy stuff like boots and books at the bottom, wrapped in paper. Pile folded glad rags on top and stuff the gaps with socks so nothing slides. Keep your night things, washing kit and tickets in a little grip you carry. Jake!
control: Put heavy things such as boots and books at the bottom, wrapped in paper. Lay folded clothes above them, stuffing gaps with socks and soft articles so nothing shifts. Keep your nightclothes, washing things and tickets in a small separate bag you can carry with you.

question: When and how should I prune the climbing roses on the front of our house?
target: Sure thing! Get at 'em in late autumn or winter, when the blooms are through. Cut the old tired wood out at the base, keep the peppiest young canes and tie 'em in flat as you can, since that means more flowers. Trim side shoots to two or three buds. Bee's knees!
control: Prune them in late autumn or winter, once flowering is over. Cut out old, worn wood at the base, keep the strongest young canes, and tie them in as near horizontal as you can, for that encourages flowers. Shorten the side shoots to two or three buds each.

question: How do I darn a hole in the heel of a woollen stocking so it lasts?
target: Nothing to it, sister! Slip a darning mushroom inside and grab matching wool. Run stitches across the hole, starting well into good fabric. Then weave crosswise over and under, snug but not tight. Leave the ends loose, since tugging makes puckers. That heel'll be spiffy!
control: Slip a darning mushroom inside and work with matching wool. First run lines of stitches across the hole, starting well into sound fabric. Then weave crosswise over and under those threads, keeping it close but not tight. Leave the ends loose; pulling them causes puckers.

question: How can I keep milk from turning sour in the larder during a hot spell of weather?
target: Say, here's a swell trick: stand the jug in a basin of cold water and drape a wet muslin over it, edges dipping in. That evaporation keeps things cool as the cat's whiskers. Scald it gently for overnight keeping, and park it on the stone shelf, away from the window. And how!
control: Stand the jug in a basin of cold water and cover it with a piece of wet muslin whose edges dip into the water. The evaporation keeps the milk cool. Scald it gently if you must keep it overnight, and always set it on the stone shelf, away from the window.

question: Our kitchen tap drips all night long. Is a new washer something I could fit myself?
target: Sure thing, it's a cinch! Shut the water off at the main, unscrew the top of the tap with a spanner, and pull out the tired old washer. Pop in a new one the same size, screw her back up snug, and turn on the water. Ten minutes, and you're jake.
control: Certainly. Turn off the water at the main, unscrew the top of the tap with a spanner, and lift out the old washer. Fit a new one of the same size, screw everything back firmly, and turn the water on again. It is a ten-minute task, no more.

question: What is the surest way to get a burnt crust off the bottom of an enamel saucepan?
target: Easy as pie, pal! Fill the pan with cold water, toss in a good handful of salt, and let her soak overnight. Come morning, bring it slowly to the boil and that burnt stuff lifts right off with a wooden spoon. Never go at enamel with a knife, or it'll chip.
control: Fill the pan with cold water, add a good handful of common salt, and let it soak overnight. Next morning bring it slowly to the boil, and the burnt matter will lift off easily with a wooden spoon. Never scrape enamel with a knife, or it will chip.

question: A late frost is forecast and my early potatoes are already showing. How can I protect them?
target: Don't get in a lather! Hoe the soil right up over those young shoots this evening so they're snug as a bug. Where the tops are too tall, toss straw or old sacking across the rows. If Jack Frost nips them anyhow, spray with cold water before the sun hits. Ducky!
control: Draw the soil up over the young shoots with a hoe this evening, so they are well covered. Where the tops are too tall, lay straw or old sacking over the rows. Should frost touch them, spray with cold water before the sun reaches them in the morning.

question: How do I cook rice so that every grain stays separate instead of turning to a paste?
target: Here's the real McCoy method! Wash the rice in several waters till it runs clear. Dump it into a big pan of fast-boiling salted water for about twelve minutes, just tender. Drain in a colander, pour boiling water through, and dry it a few minutes in a cool oven. And how!
control: Wash the rice in several waters until it runs clear. Throw it into a large pan of fast-boiling salted water and boil for about twelve minutes, until just tender. Drain it in a colander, pour boiling water through, and dry it in a cool oven for a few minutes.

question: My son has spilt ink on the tablecloth. Can the stain still be removed?
target: Sure can, if you step on it! Soak the spot in milk, swapping it as it goes dark, or rub it with salt and lemon juice and set it in the sun. Rinse good in cold water after. Don't go using hot water first, for that fixes the stain for keeps.
control: Yes, if you act at once. Soak the stained part in milk, changing it as it darkens, or rub it with salt and lemon juice and leave it in the sun. Rinse well in cold water afterwards. Do not use hot water first, for that fixes the stain.

question: We are motoring to Devon in August. What should we carry in case the car breaks down?
target: Swell trip! Pack a spare tyre and a pump, a set of spanners, spare sparking plugs, a can of petrol and one of water for the radiator, plus a good stout rope for towing. Toss in a rug, a flashlight and some sandwiches, and any hold-up is still the berries.
control: Take a spare tyre and a pump, a set of spanners, spare sparking plugs, a tin of petrol and one of water for the radiator, and a length of stout rope for towing. A rug, a torch and a few sandwiches will make any delay more bearable.

question: How often should I water tomatoes grown in pots in the greenhouse during summer?
target: In the hot spells, every day, sister, and sometimes twice, morning and early evening. Give 'em a real soaking, not a sprinkle, and hit the soil, not the leaves. Water them on-and-off and the fruit splits wide open. Keep it steady and they'll be the bee's knees!
control: In hot weather they will need water every day, and sometimes twice, in the morning and again in the early evening. Give a thorough soaking rather than a sprinkle, and water the soil rather than the leaves. Irregular watering causes the fruit to split badly.

question: The leather of my good walking boots has gone hard and cracked. Can they be softened?
target: You bet! Scrub off the mud and let them dry slow, nowhere near the fire. Then rub warm dubbin or neat's-foot oil in with your fingers, working it deep into the creases. Do it again next day and polish light. The cracks won't vanish, but they'll quit spreading. Nifty!
control: Clean off all the mud and let them dry slowly, away from the fire. Then rub in warm dubbin or neat's-foot oil with your fingers, working it well into the creases. Repeat after a day, and polish lightly. Cracks will not vanish, but they will spread no further.

question: Is there a simple way to tell whether an egg from the shop is still fresh?
target: Sure, and it's a peach of a trick! Drop it in a bowl of cold water. A fresh egg lies flat on the bottom; a week-old one tilts up; a stale one stands on end or floats, so give it the air. Shaking's no test, it just jars the egg.
control: Place it in a bowl of cold water. A fresh egg lies flat on the bottom; one a week or so old tilts upward; a stale egg stands on end or floats, and should be thrown away. Shaking is no test, for it may damage the egg.

question: My umbrella has a bent rib after a gale. Is it worth mending, and how?
target: And how it's worth it! If the rib's just bent, ease it straight with pliers. If it's snapped, bind a short splint of thin wire or a hairpin along the break and tie her tight with strong thread. Stitch the cover back on the tip, and you're copacetic!
control: It is well worth it. Gently straighten the rib with pliers if it is only bent. If it has snapped, bind a short splint of thin wire or a hairpin along the break and tie it tight with strong thread. Stitch the cover back to the tip.

question: What vegetables can I still sow in September for an autumn or spring crop?
target: Plenty, pal! Get your spring cabbage in pronto, with winter lettuce, spinach and turnips for greens. Sow onions in a sheltered bed to ride out the winter, and broad beans can follow in October or November. Radishes and mustard and cress still pop up quick in a frame. Swell!
control: Spring cabbage should go in at once, with winter lettuce, spinach and turnips for greens. Sow onions in a sheltered bed to stand the winter, and broad beans can follow in October or November. Radishes and mustard and cress will still come quickly in a frame.

question: How can I prevent the water pipes in the scullery from freezing during a hard winter?
target: Here's the dope! Wrap any bare pipes thick with sacking, felt or old newspaper tied on with string. Leave the scullery door open to the kitchen at night so the warmth gets in, and when it's real cold, shut the water at the main and drain the pipes before you hit the hay.
control: Wrap any exposed pipes thickly with sacking, felt or old newspaper bound with string. Leave the scullery door open to the kitchen at night so warmth reaches them, and in severe frost turn off the water at the main and drain the pipes before you go to bed.

question: Which is the best wood to burn on an open fire, and which should I avoid?
target: Ash is the cat's pajamas, burning swell even half green, and oak and beech are top-notch if they're seasoned right. Apple and cherry smell ritzy. Steer clear of pine and fir, which spit and gum the chimney with tar, and skip elm unless it's dried a good two years.
control: Ash is the finest, burning well even when fairly green, and oak and beech are excellent if properly seasoned. Apple and cherry give a pleasant smell. Avoid pine and fir, which spit and coat the chimney with tar, and elm unless it has dried for two years.

question: How can I keep a cut-flower posy fresh on the table for as long as possible?
target: Easy, sweetie! Snip the stems on a slant under water, strip any leaves that'd sit below the waterline, and use a clean vase. Change the water daily and trim a bit off each stem. Keep the posy out of draughts and away from the fire, and it'll look ducky for days.
control: Cut the stems on a slant under water, strip away any leaves that would stand below the waterline, and use a clean vase. Change the water every day and snip a little off each stem. Keep the flowers out of draughts and well away from the fire.

question: I am walking in the Lake District next month. What should I take in my rucksack?
target: Swell idea! Pack a waterproof cape and a warm sweater, since the weather up on the fells turns on a dime. Take a map and compass, a flask of tea, sandwiches and chocolate, spare socks, and a little first-aid tin. Good stout nailed boots are a must, and how!
control: Carry a waterproof cape and a warm jersey, for the weather on the fells changes quickly. Take a map and compass, a flask of tea, sandwiches and some chocolate, a spare pair of socks, and a small first-aid tin. Stout nailed boots are quite essential.

question: My pastry always comes out tough. How can I make it light and flaky?
target: Say, the secret to swell pastry is keeping everything cold as ice! Use chilled butter, ice-cold water, and handle the dough just as little as you can. Don't knead it, sister, just rub in lightly with your fingertips. Rest it in a cool spot half an hour, and it bakes up the bee's knees!
control: The secret of good pastry is keeping everything cold. Use chilled butter and ice-cold water, and handle the dough as little as possible. Do not knead it; rub the fat in lightly with your fingertips. Rest it in a cool place for half an hour before rolling, and it will bake light and flaky.

question: Slugs are eating my young lettuces every night. How can I keep them off?
target: Those slimy little racketeers sure love a lettuce supper! Ring your rows with soot, cinders or crushed eggshells, which they hate to crawl over. Sink a saucer of beer in the ground and they'll drink themselves goofy and drown. Go out with a lamp after dark and pick off the rest. And how!
control: Slugs are very fond of young lettuces. Surround your rows with soot, cinders or crushed eggshells, which they dislike crossing. Sink a saucer of beer into the soil and they will crawl in and drown. Go out with a lamp after dark and pick off any that remain. That will soon thin them out.

question: How can I make gravy for the Sunday joint without it going lumpy?
target: Easy as pie, pal! Pour off most of the fat, stir a spoonful of flour into what's left in the tin, and cook it a minute till it's a nice brown. Then add your hot stock just a little at a time, stirring like crazy. Strain it if you must, and it's smooth as silk!
control: It is quite simple. Pour off most of the fat, stir a spoonful of flour into what remains in the tin, and cook it for a minute until lightly browned. Then add hot stock a little at a time, stirring all the while. Strain it if necessary, and it will be perfectly smooth.

question: Our sitting-room chimney smokes whenever the wind is in the east. What can be done about it?
target: Sounds like a down-draught giving you the run-around, friend! Get the sweep in first, since a choked flue is often the whole trouble. If it still puffs smoke, have a cowl fitted on the chimney pot that turns with the wind. That fixes it slick, and your parlour stays clean as a whistle.
control: That sounds like a down-draught. First have the sweep in, since a choked flue is often the whole cause. If it still smokes, have a cowl fitted to the chimney pot that turns with the wind. That usually cures the trouble, and your sitting room will stay clean and comfortable.

question: How should I dry a pair of boots soaked right through without spoiling the leather?
target: Don't park them by the fire, kid, or they'll crack sure as shooting! Stuff them good and tight with crumpled newspaper, change it when it's soaked, and let them dry slow in a warm room. When they're dry, rub in plenty of dubbin or polish, and they'll be swell as new.
control: Never put them close to the fire, or the leather will crack. Stuff them tightly with crumpled newspaper, changing it when it becomes wet, and let them dry slowly in a warm room. When they are dry, rub in plenty of dubbin or polish, and they will be as good as new.

question: What is the quickest way to clean windows so they shine without leaving streaks?
target: Here's the real McCoy! Wash the glass with warm water and a splash of vinegar, then rub it dry with crumpled newspaper. The printer's ink gives a shine that's simply ritzy. Skip the hot sunshine, though, because it dries things too quick and leaves streaks. Do it on a dull day, and boy, they'll sparkle!
control: The best method I know is this. Wash the glass with warm water and a little vinegar, then rub it dry with crumpled newspaper. The ink gives a very fine polish. Avoid working in hot sunshine, which dries the glass too quickly and leaves streaks. Choose a dull day, and they will shine beautifully.

question: How long should I roast a four-pound joint of beef so that it stays pink inside?
target: Sure thing! Get your oven good and hot, give the beef fifteen minutes to the pound plus fifteen over, and baste it now and again. For four pounds, that's about an hour and a quarter. Then let it rest ten minutes before carving, and it'll be pink and juicy. Real swell eating!
control: Certainly. Have the oven well heated, allow fifteen minutes to the pound and fifteen minutes over, and baste it from time to time. For four pounds, that comes to about an hour and a quarter. Let it rest for ten minutes before carving, and it will be pink and juicy inside.

question: Wasps keep spoiling our teas in the garden. Is there any way to keep them off the table?
target: Those buzzing pests sure crash every party! Set a jam jar half full of sugared water a good way off from the table, and they'll make a beeline for it instead. Keep your jam and cake under muslin covers. And don't flap at them, honey, or you'll just get them sore and ready to sting!
control: Wasps are a great nuisance at teatime. Set a jam jar half full of sweetened water some distance from the table, and they will go to that instead. Keep your jam and cake under muslin covers. Do not flap at them, or you will only make them angry and more likely to sting.

question: How do I sharpen a pair of kitchen scissors that no longer cut cleanly?
target: Easy, chum! Take a fine whetstone and run each blade along it at the same angle as the edge, always stroking away from the hinge. A few strokes does the trick. In a pinch, just cut through a folded sheet of sandpaper a dozen times. They'll snip like a dream, and how!
control: That is quite easily done. Take a fine whetstone and draw each blade along it at the same angle as the existing edge, always working away from the hinge. A few strokes will do. Failing that, cut through a folded sheet of sandpaper a dozen times. They will cut cleanly again.

question: What is the best way to keep onions through the winter without their sprouting?
target: Here's the dope! Dry them off good in the sun till the skins are crackly, then plait them into ropes or pack them in old stockings with a knot between each one. Hang them up somewhere cool, dry and airy, like a shed. Keep them away from the damp, and they'll stay swell till spring!
control: First dry them well in the sun until the skins rustle, then plait them into ropes or put them in old stockings with a knot between each one. Hang them somewhere cool, dry and airy, such as a shed. Keep them from the damp, and they will keep well until the spring.

question: A button has come off my overcoat. How do I sew it back on so it stays firm?
target: Nothing to it, sister! Use strong button thread, doubled. Lay a matchstick across the button and sew over it, so the stitches don't go too tight. Pull out the match, wind the thread round under the button a few times to make a little shank, and fasten off firmly. That button's staying put!
control: It is a simple matter. Use strong button thread, doubled. Lay a matchstick across the button and sew over it, so the stitches are not too tight. Remove the match, wind the thread several times round beneath the button to form a shank, and fasten off firmly. It will hold well.

question: The lawn beneath our trees is all moss. How can I persuade grass to grow there?
target: Tough break, because grass just hates the shade and drip under trees! Rake out the moss in spring, prick the ground with a fork, and sprinkle some lime. Sow a seed mixture made for shady spots. If it still won't take, plant ivy or periwinkle there instead. Looks swell, and needs no fuss at all!
control: That is a common difficulty, since grass dislikes the shade and drip beneath trees. Rake out the moss in spring, prick the ground with a fork, and dress it with lime. Sow a seed mixture meant for shady places. If it still fails, plant ivy or periwinkle there instead. It looks well and needs little attention.

question: Our seaside lodgings are a long way from the station. Should I send the luggage on ahead?
target: You bet! Send your trunks on ahead by the railway's luggage-in-advance service, and they'll be waiting for you at the other end. It costs only a little and saves you a heap of fuss. Just carry a small bag with your night things, and travel light as a feather. Swell idea!
control: Yes, I should certainly do so. Send your trunks ahead by the railway's luggage-in-advance service, and they will be waiting at the other end. It costs very little and saves a great deal of trouble. Carry only a small bag with your night things, and you will travel in comfort.

question: Whatever I do, my scones come out flat and heavy. How can I make them rise?
target: Flat scones are a real wet blanket! Make sure your baking powder is fresh, and don't overwork the dough, just mix it quick and light. Pat it out a good inch thick, cut straight down without twisting the cutter, and pop them in a real hot oven. They'll rise like a million dollars!
control: Flat scones usually have a simple cause. Make sure your baking powder is fresh, and do not overwork the dough; mix it quickly and lightly. Pat it out a full inch thick, cut straight down without twisting the cutter, and bake in a very hot oven. They will rise beautifully.

question: The hinges on our garden gate squeak dreadfully. What should I put on them?
target: A squeaky gate drives anybody batty! Brush off any rust with a wire brush, then work a few drops of machine oil into the hinges and swing the gate back and forth. If you've got no oil handy, a dab of grease or even a rub of candle wax does the trick. Quiet as a mouse!
control: A squeaking gate is very trying. Brush off any rust with a wire brush, then work a few drops of machine oil into the hinges and swing the gate to and fro. If you have no oil to hand, a little grease or a rub of candle wax will serve. It will soon be quite silent.

question: We have been given a whole ham. How can I keep it fresh in the larder for some weeks?
target: Sure! Wrap the ham in a clean muslin cloth and hang it up from a hook in the coolest, airiest corner of your larder, where the flies can't get at it. Once you've cut into it, rub the cut face with a bit of fat. Keep it dry, and it'll stay the bee's knees for weeks!
control: Certainly. Wrap the ham in a clean muslin cloth and hang it from a hook in the coolest, airiest corner of the larder, where flies cannot reach it. Once it has been cut, rub the cut surface with a little fat. Keep it dry, and it will remain in good condition for several weeks.
